body:
Why nuclear technology requires international cooperation

Nuclear energy is obtained from changes within the nucleus of an atom. In a nuclear power station, controlled nuclear fission releases heat, which is used to produce electricity. Nuclear technology also has peaceful applications in medicine, agriculture, industry and scientific research.

However, some nuclear materials, technologies and specialised knowledge have both peaceful and military applications. This is called the dual-use character of nuclear technology. A country may legitimately develop nuclear electricity, but international cooperation must also address the possibility that nuclear material or technology could be diverted towards nuclear weapons.

International nuclear governance therefore tries to achieve 2 related objectives: enable peaceful nuclear development and reduce the risks associated with nuclear technology. These objectives require cooperation among governments, international organisations, nuclear suppliers and national regulatory authorities.

Three different concerns: safety, security and safeguards

The words nuclear safety, nuclear security and nuclear safeguards describe different responsibilities. They should not be used interchangeably.

  • Nuclear safety: Preventing accidents, controlling radiation exposure and reducing the harmful consequences of accidental releases of radioactive material. Safety measures protect workers, the public and the environment.
  • Nuclear security: Protecting nuclear material and facilities against theft, sabotage, unauthorised access and other deliberate malicious acts.
  • Nuclear safeguards: Verifying that nuclear material and facilities covered by international agreements are not diverted from permitted peaceful purposes to nuclear weapons or other nuclear explosive devices.

For example, checking whether a plant can safely withstand a natural disaster is a safety matter. Protecting its radioactive material against theft is a security matter. Verifying the declared quantity and use of safeguarded nuclear material is a safeguards matter.

The International Atomic Energy Agency

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) was established in 1957. Its headquarters is in Vienna, Austria. It is an autonomous intergovernmental organisation associated with the United Nations system.

The IAEA promotes the peaceful use of nuclear science and technology, develops international nuclear safety standards, supports technical cooperation and implements safeguards under agreements concluded with states. Its safeguards activities contribute to the international effort to prevent nuclear proliferation.

The IAEA does not replace a country's government or nuclear regulatory authority. Nuclear installations remain subject to national laws and regulatory decisions. The IAEA's power to conduct safeguards verification depends on the applicable legal agreements; membership in the IAEA alone does not automatically place every nuclear facility under inspection.

Central distinction: Safety addresses accidental harm, security addresses deliberate hostile acts, and safeguards address the diversion of nuclear material from permitted uses.

Prelims focus

  • IAEA was established in 1957.
  • IAEA headquarters: Vienna, Austria.
  • IAEA safeguards primarily support nuclear non-proliferation through verification.
  • Nuclear safety and nuclear safeguards are different functions.
  • National authorities retain responsibility for regulating nuclear safety.
  • Trap: IAEA membership does not automatically mean that all facilities in a country are subject to IAEA safeguards.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12 Political Science, Contemporary World Politics, chapter International Organisations, printed p. 94; IAEA, The Legal Framework for IAEA Safeguards, summary and section The IAEA Statute, September 2024; IAEA, Nuclear Safety and Security Frequently Asked Questions, entries dated 23 March 2024 and 15 October 2022; consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Peaceful Nuclear Energy and the Need for International Rules

body:
What international nuclear safeguards mean

IAEA safeguards are technical verification measures applied under legal agreements to check whether nuclear material and specified nuclear activities are being used consistently with a state's peaceful-use commitments.

Safeguards are based on evidence, not merely on declarations of intention. A state provides information required by its safeguards agreement, and the IAEA checks that information using the verification measures authorised by the agreement.

Typical safeguards activities include examination of nuclear-material records, verification of declared material quantities, inspections of facilities, environmental sampling, and the use of seals or surveillance equipment. The precise measures depend on the facility, the nuclear material involved and the applicable safeguards agreement.

The purpose is to detect and deter diversion and to provide safeguards conclusions supported by the verification evidence. An inspection is not a general search of every military or industrial establishment in a country.

The main types of safeguards agreements

Agreement typeGenerally applies toScope
Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement (CSA)Non-nuclear-weapon states party to the NPTAll nuclear material in all peaceful nuclear activities covered by the agreement
Voluntary Offer Agreement (VOA)The 5 nuclear-weapon states recognised under the NPTMaterial in eligible facilities offered by the state and selected for safeguards
Item-specific safeguards agreementStates or arrangements involving specified nuclear material, facilities or itemsThe material and items identified in the agreement

A Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement is commonly associated with the obligations of non-nuclear-weapon states that have joined the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. It does not mean that the IAEA directly operates the state's nuclear establishments.

An Additional Protocol is a separate legal instrument that supplements a safeguards agreement. It may give the IAEA wider access to information and locations, strengthening its ability to assess whether nuclear activities have been declared as required. Its precise provisions depend on the agreement concerned. It should not be confused with a comprehensive safeguards agreement itself.

India's safeguards arrangements

India is not a party to the NPT and does not have an NPT-style comprehensive safeguards agreement covering all its nuclear material in peaceful activities. Instead, India has safeguards arrangements applying to specified facilities and material.

The India-specific Agreement for the Application of Safeguards to Civilian Nuclear Facilities, published as INFCIRC/754, was signed on 2 February 2009 and entered into force on 11 May 2009. India's Additional Protocol entered into force on 25 July 2014.

These arrangements are particularly important for India's international civil nuclear cooperation. They allow the IAEA to verify nuclear material and facilities brought under the relevant safeguards commitments. They do not make every Indian nuclear facility, including facilities outside the declared civilian arrangements, subject to comprehensive safeguards.

Who is responsible for nuclear safety?

The operator of a nuclear installation has the primary responsibility for the safety of that installation. The national government establishes the legal and regulatory framework, while the national nuclear regulator authorises, inspects and oversees activities according to domestic law.

The IAEA develops safety standards and offers international review and assistance. However, it does not have a general mandate to enforce its safety standards inside every country. A country may use IAEA standards when developing its regulatory requirements, but this is different from an IAEA safeguards inspection.

In India, the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) is the national regulatory body associated with nuclear and radiation safety. The IAEA and the AERB therefore perform different functions.

Safeguards compliance is not the same as plant safety. A facility may have its nuclear material correctly accounted for under safeguards and still require independent assessment of accident prevention, radiation protection, emergency preparedness and waste management.

Prelims focus

  • Comprehensive safeguards generally cover all nuclear material in peaceful activities of an NPT non-nuclear-weapon state.
  • Item-specific safeguards apply to material or facilities identified by the agreement.
  • An Additional Protocol supplements a safeguards agreement.
  • India's civilian safeguards agreement entered into force on 11 May 2009.
  • India's Additional Protocol entered into force on 25 July 2014.
  • Trap: India's safeguards agreement does not place its entire nuclear programme under IAEA comprehensive safeguards.

[Sources: IAEA, The Legal Framework for IAEA Safeguards, sections Types of Safeguards Agreements and Protocols to Safeguards Agreements, September 2024; IAEA Office of Legal Affairs, India Country Factsheet, Safeguards Agreements, entries for 2009 and 2014; IAEA, Nuclear Safety and Security Frequently Asked Questions, 23 March 2024; consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
The purpose of the NPT

The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) is a major international treaty intended to prevent the further spread of nuclear weapons, support cooperation in peaceful uses of nuclear energy and advance nuclear disarmament.

The NPT opened for signature on 1 July 1968 and entered into force on 5 March 1970. In 1995, its parties agreed to extend the treaty indefinitely. This indefinite extension did not mean that the treaty's disarmament commitments had already been fulfilled.

The 3 principal objectives

  • Non-proliferation: Prevent the transfer or acquisition of nuclear weapons by additional states.
  • Peaceful nuclear cooperation: Recognise the right of parties to pursue peaceful nuclear research, production and use, consistently with their non-proliferation obligations.
  • Nuclear disarmament: Require parties to pursue negotiations in good faith on effective measures relating to nuclear disarmament and the cessation of the nuclear arms race.

Important articles and their meanings

ArticleMain provisionImportant distinction
Article INuclear-weapon-state parties must not transfer nuclear weapons or assist non-nuclear-weapon states in acquiring them.Concerned with obligations of nuclear-weapon states
Article IINon-nuclear-weapon-state parties must not receive, manufacture or otherwise acquire nuclear weapons.Concerned with obligations of non-nuclear-weapon states
Article IIINon-nuclear-weapon-state parties undertake to accept IAEA safeguards under a comprehensive safeguards agreement covering all nuclear material in their peaceful nuclear activities.Links NPT obligations with IAEA verification
Article IVRecognises the right to peaceful nuclear research, production and use, in conformity with Articles I and II.Peaceful use is permitted, subject to treaty obligations
Article VIRequires good-faith negotiations on nuclear disarmament and related measures.Disarmament is a treaty objective and obligation

Which states are recognised as nuclear-weapon states?

Article IX of the NPT defines a nuclear-weapon state as a state that manufactured and exploded a nuclear weapon or other nuclear explosive device before 1 January 1967.

Under this treaty definition, the 5 recognised nuclear-weapon states are the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, France and China. Russia occupies the relevant treaty position formerly held by the Soviet Union.

This definition is historical and legal. It does not mean that only 5 states possess nuclear weapons. A country may possess nuclear weapons but still not qualify as a nuclear-weapon state under the NPT definition.

India and the NPT

India is not a party to the NPT. India has objected to the treaty's unequal distinction between countries whose nuclear-weapon status is recognised under the historical cutoff and those outside that category. India has supported the objective of universal, non-discriminatory nuclear disarmament while remaining outside the treaty.

India's possession of nuclear weapons does not give it the legal status of a recognised nuclear-weapon state under the NPT. At the same time, being outside the NPT does not mean that every form of peaceful nuclear cooperation with India is prohibited. Such cooperation depends on the applicable export-control decisions, safeguards arrangements and bilateral agreements.

Do not confuse treaty recognition with physical possession. The NPT recognises 5 nuclear-weapon states using a date-based definition; India is a nuclear-armed state but is not one of those 5 NPT-recognised states.

Prelims focus

  • NPT opened for signature: 1 July 1968.
  • NPT entered into force: 5 March 1970.
  • NPT was extended indefinitely in 1995.
  • Article III connects NPT non-nuclear-weapon-state obligations with IAEA safeguards.
  • Article VI concerns negotiations towards nuclear disarmament.
  • Trap: The NPT's nuclear-weapon-state cutoff is before 1 January 1967, not the date on which the treaty entered into force.

[Sources: United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs, Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, overview and review-conference history; IAEA, Safeguards Glossary, 2022 edition, section Treaties and Supply Agreements, entry on the NPT; IAEA, The Legal Framework for IAEA Safeguards, section Types of Safeguards Agreements, September 2024; consulted 16 November 2026.]
